o: The apostle's commission.

bg: romans, epistle to the

This epistle was probably written at Corinth. Phoebe (Rom. 16:1) of Cenchrea conveyed it to Rome, and Gaius of Corinth entertained the apostle at the time of his writing it (16:23; 1 Cor. 1:14), and Erastus was chamberlain of the city, i.e., of Corinth (2 Tim. 4:20).
Rome

Jewish inhabitants. the conquests of Pompey seem to have given rise to the first settlement of Jews at Rome. The Jewish king Aristobulus and his son formed part of Pompey's triumph, and many Jewish captives and immigrants were brought to Rome at that time.
Paul
We read of his sister and his sister's son (Acts 23:16), and of other relatives (Rom. 16:7, 11, 12). Though a Jew, his father was a Roman citizen.
ch.s: This chapter covers: The apostle's commission (vv. 1–7); Prays for the saints at Rome, and expresses his desire to see them (vv. 8–15); The gospel way of justification by faith, for Jews and Gentiles (vv. 16,17); The sins of the Gentiles set forth (vv. 18–32). People named: Rome, Paul, David, Jew.
ch.mh: The doctrine of which the apostle Paul wrote, set forth the fulfilment of the promises by the prophets.
q: Read verses 1–7 (The apostle's commission). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 8–15 (Prays for the saints at Rome, and expresses his desire to see them), what do you learn about faith and trust?
Verse 16 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Mark 8:38. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Rome’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of wisdom in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Romans?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: We should readily impart to others what God has trusted to us, rejoicing to make others joyful, especially taking pleasure in communing with those who believe the same things with us.
ch.a: Name one worry and deliberately hand it over to God in prayer each day this week.

Spain

Paul expresses his intention (Rom. 15:24, 28) to visit Spain. There is, however, no evidence that he ever carried it into effect, although some think that he probably did so between his first and second imprisonment.
Illyricum

A country to the north-west of Macedonia, on the eastern shores of the Adriatic, now almost wholly comprehended in Dalmatia, a name formerly given to the southern part of Illyricum (2 Tim. 4:10). It was traversed by Paul in his third missionary journey (Rom. 15:19).

People named: Esaias, Jesse. Places: Jerusalem, Spain, Illyricum, Macedonia, Achaia.
ch.mh: Christian liberty was allowed, not for our pleasure, but for the glory of God, and the good of others.

bg: romans, epistle to the

This epistle was probably written at Corinth. Phoebe (Rom. 16:1) of Cenchrea conveyed it to Rome, and Gaius of Corinth entertained the apostle at the time of his writing it (16:23; 1 Cor. 1:14), and Erastus was chamberlain of the city, i.e., of Corinth (2 Tim. 4:20).
Achaia

(trouble) signifies in the New Testament a Roman province which included the whole of the Peloponnesus and the greater part of Hellas proper, with the adjacent islands. This province, with that of Macedonia, comprehended the while of Greece; hence Achaia and Macedonia are frequently mentioned together in the New Testament to indicate all Greece.
Phebe
A "deaconess of the church at Cenchrea," the port of Corinth. She was probably the bearer of Paul's epistle to the Romans.
Cenchrea

Millet, the eastern harbour of Corinth, from which it was distant about 9 miles east, and the outlet for its trade with the Asiatic shores of the Mediterranean. When Paul returned from his second missionary journey to Syria, he sailed from this port (Acts 18:18).

People named: Phebe, Cenchrea, Priscilla, Aquila, Epenetus, Mary. Places: Achaia.
